Ground states of quantum XY dipoles on the Archimedean lattices

Marcus Bintz∗ Affiliation: Department of Physics, Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts 02138, USA    Ahmed Khalifa∗ Affiliation: Department of Physics, Carnegie Mellon University, Pittsburgh, PA 15213, USA    Vincent S. Liu Affiliation: Department of Physics, Harvard University, Cambridge, Massachusetts 02138, USA    Johannes Hauschild Affiliation: Technical University of Munich, TUM School of Natural Sciences, Physics Department, James-Franck-Str. 1, 85748 Garching, Germany Affiliation: Munich Center for Quantum Science and Technology (MCQST), Schellingstr. 4, 80799 München, Germany    Michael P. Zaletel Affiliation: Department of Physics, University of California, Berkeley, CA 94720, USA Affiliation: Material Science Division, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Berkeley, CA 94720, USA    Shubhayu Chatterjee Affiliation: Department of Physics, Carnegie Mellon University, Pittsburgh, PA 15213, USA    Norman Y. August 24, 2026
Abstract

We report numerical ground states for the dipolar XY spin model, which describes extended antiferromagnetic interactions in two-dimensional arrays of polar molecules and two-level Rydberg atoms. Carrying out large-scale density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) calculations, we compute ground state properties on nine of the eleven Archimedean lattices—tilings of the plane by regular polygons. Four of these host trivial paramagnets, while another four develop collinear Neél magnetic order, as was found previously for the square lattice. For the ordered states, we calculate the hydrodynamic parameters (magnetization, susceptibility, and stiffness) and compare to linear spin wave theory. We also investigate the triangular lattice, for which we find several competing phases including coplanar magnetism, stripe density wave order, and a possible spin liquid; their relative stability is sensitive to the long-range couplings present in our dipolar model. Finally, the Archimedean classification is completed by the kagome lattice, which we argue in a companion work is likely to be a Dirac spin liquid.

I Introduction

Geometry is essential to matter: two collections of microscopic particles with the same elemental composition and fundamental interactions, differing only in their spatial arrangement, will often have completely different macroscopic material properties. Even minimalistic systems exhibit this sensitivity; a well-known example is the Heisenberg model of S=1/2S=1/2 spins coupled by local spin-exchange on a two-dimensional lattice [58]. When placed on the vertices of square tiling, such spins develop conventional, collinear antiferromagnetic order at low temperature [50, 73]. But if one simply begins with a different tiling of the plane—such as with hexagons and corner-sharing triangles—wholly distinct phases of matter can emerge, possibly including exotic quantum spin liquids [21, 53, 76, 63].

Geometry is also increasingly a domain under experimental control. One especially exciting area of development is in ultracold atom and molecule experiments, where it is now possible to orchestrate large arrays of individually-positioned, tightly focused laser beams that each trap single particles  [41, 5, 22, 38]. In such highly-configurable optical tweezer arrays [46, 14, 34], the lattice spacing is typically on the order of several microns—this has key consequences for the natural interactions at play. Namely, tunneling-induced exchange is exponentially suppressed, and the most relevant inter-particle couplings are instead mediated by the ambient electromagnetic field [9]. These can be maximized by employing particles with large local moments, e.g. polar molecules or Rydberg atoms.

A native Hamiltonian commonly arising in such experiments is the spin-1/2 dipolar XY model,

HdXY=J​∑i<jSi+​Sj−+Si−​Sj+(ri​j/a)3H_{\rm{dXY}}=J\sum_{i<j}\frac{S_{i}^{+}S_{j}^{-}+S_{i}^{-}S_{j}^{+}}{(r_{ij}/a)^{3}} (1)

which describes the dipole-dipole interaction [31] between atomic [47, 8, 23] or molecular [4, 43, 59, 33, 15] qubits possessing a large internal transition dipole moment, but no permanent moment (i.e. due to parity symmetry). Here, ri​jr_{ij} is the distance between spins ii and jj, aa is a microscopic length scale (lattice spacing), and JJ is the coupling constant; we focus here on the antiferromagnetic case, J>0J>0. The dipolar XY Hamiltonian has no free parameters, and so its ground state is completely determined by the geometric arrangement of the atoms or molecules.

We are thus motivated to investigate the geometry-dependence of the HdXYH_{\rm{dXY}} ground state. Experimentally, there is already evidence that a simple square lattice arrangement leads to an ordered state, spontaneously breaking the continuous U⁡(1)U(1) symmetry generated by the conserved magnetization Mz=∑iSizM_{z}=\sum_{i}S_{i}^{z} [11, 56, 64]. By contrast, in a companion work we numerically show that on the kagome lattice, strong geometric frustration leads to a disordered state, likely to be the gapless Dirac spin liquid [6]. Both of these two-dimensional geometries are examples of so-called Archimedean lattices, formed by tilings of regular polygons where all vertices are symmetry-equivalent [58, 26]. There are eleven such planar arrangements—in this paper, we study the ground state of HdXYH_{\rm{dXY}} on the remaining nine.

Carrying out large-scale density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) calculations [74, 69, 30], we find these states fall into two general classes, with one exception. The first common phase is collinear U⁡(1)U(1) symmetry breaking order, evinced by long-range ⟨Six​Sjx⟩\langle S^{x}_{i}S^{x}_{j}\rangle correlations with a clear Neél sign structure. This occurs when frustration is weak: on the square, hexagonal, truncated square, snub square, and truncated trihexagonal lattices (Sec. II). In these cases, the order can be captured analytically by semiclassical linear spin wave theory; this has three characteristic hydrodynamic parameters, which we can also compute with DMRG (Sec. III).

A second possibility arises for more frustrated systems but with an even number of spins per unit cell: the elongated triangular, truncated hexagonal, rhombitrihexagonal, and snub trihexagonal lattices (Sec. IV). On these geometries, neighboring spins form local two- or six-spin singlet states, and the full many-body wavefunction is a trivial paramagnet, i.e. to good approximation, a tensor product of the local singlets. Finally, for the triangular lattice we find that several phases closely compete in energy, including conventional coplanar order and a possible spin liquid (Sec. V).

II Collinear antiferromagnets

In this section, we introduce the four lattices which numerically are found to have collinear antiferromagnetic order. We first present the results from infinite DMRG (iDMRG) calculations, and then discuss our formalism (linear spin wave theory) for analytically understanding this order. The quantitative calculation of the characteristic hydrodynamic parameters for these orders is done afterwards in Section III.

II.1 iDMRG

We compute the ground state of HdXYH_{\rm{dXY}} with iDMRG, making use of the TeNPy library [30]. In order to apply the one-dimensional iDMRG algorithm, we compactify the plane into a cylinder with infinite length, and finite circumference WW. Additionally, the full long-range interactions cannot be exactly represented in the iDMRG setting; there is also some ambiguity in how the multiple paths around the cylinder should be accounted for. We choose to simply truncate, so that only sites with distance ri​j<Rmax=W/2r_{ij}<R_{\mathrm{max}}=W/2 are coupled, and the coupling strength only includes the contribution from the shortest-distance path. This and other choices of prescription for the interactions converge in the thermodynamic W→∞W\to\infty limit, but at finite WW there can be quantitative and possibly qualitative differences in the ground state properties.

One generic possibility for the ground state is symmetry-breaking order: HdXYH_{\rm dXY} is invariant under U⁡(1)U(1) spin rotations generated by the zz-magnetization, Mz=∑iSizM^{z}=\sum_{i}S_{i}^{z}, rotations by π\pi about the xx or yy spin axes, time reversal, and any spatial symmetries of the lattice. Here, we consider states in the Mz=0M^{z}=0 sector, employing spin-conserving tensors that respect the U⁡(1)U(1) symmetry. The basic signature of spontaneous U⁡(1)U(1) symmetry breaking in this setting is off-diagonal long-range order in the ⟨Six​Sjx⟩=⟨Siy​Sjy⟩\langle S_{i}^{x}S_{j}^{x}\rangle=\langle S_{i}^{y}S_{j}^{y}\rangle correlations [77].

Five of the lattices we checked exhibited this type of order: square (not shown), hexagonal (“honeycomb”), snub square, truncated square, and truncated trihexagonal (Fig. 1c). In these lattices, the ground state ⟨Six​Sjx⟩\langle S_{i}^{x}S_{j}^{x}\rangle correlations are large and roughly constant out to long distances, before slowly decaying due to the quasi-1d infinite cylinder geometry and the finite MPS bond dimension. The correlations exhibit an obvious sign structure characteristic of a simple, bipartite Neél antiferromagnet. Such order is frustrated at the nearest-neighbor level for the snub square tiling, but only at longer distances (and hence weaker coupling) in the other four cases.

II.2 Linear spin wave theory

For the bipartite Néel antiferromagnets, we expect that a semi-classical description using linear spin wave theory (LSWT) to be reasonably accurate [2, 3]. Therefore, we briefly discuss the formalism for LSWT, and detail how to compute the long-wavelength hydrodynamic parameters [27, 28, 62], namely, the magnetization mm, the out-of-plane susceptibility χ⟂\chi_{\perp} and the spin-wave velocity vv of the acoustic mode which in turn leads to the spin-stiffness ρs=v2​χ⟂\rho_{s}=v^{2}\chi_{\perp}, enabling a comparison with the DMRG results.

The starting point of LSWT is the fully polarized Néel antiferromagnet, i.e., ⟨Sx⟩=σ​S\langle S^{x}\rangle=\sigma S, where σ=±1\sigma=\pm 1 on sublattices of type AA and type BB respectively. We denote the number of each type in the unit cell as ss (i.e. each unit cell has 2​s2s sites). We will soon supplement this, in our computation of χ⟂\chi_{\perp}, by applying an out-of-plane magnetic field hh,

H=HdXY−h​∑iSiz,H=H_{\rm dXY}-h\sum_{i}S^{z}_{i}, (2)

which leads to a uniform canting of all the spins along z^\hat{z}, i.e. a nonzero expectation value mz=⟨Siz⟩m_{z}=\langle S^{z}_{i}\rangle. Hence, it is convenient to develop LSWT in the presence of this field and set h=0h=0 to find the other hydrodynamic quantities like mm or ρs\rho_{s}.

To organize our analytic calculations, we first set some detailed notation for the lattice. We index each site with dual indices i≡(n,η)i\ \equiv(n,\eta), where 𝑹n{\bm{R}}_{n} is Bravais lattice site index and 𝒖η{\bm{u}}_{\eta} with η∈{1,2,⋯,2​s}\eta\in\{1,2,\cdots,2s\} being the sublattice index, such that 𝒓i=𝒓(n,η)=𝑹n+𝒖η{\bm{r}}_{i}={\bm{r}}_{(n,\eta)}={\bm{R}}_{n}+{\bm{u}}_{\eta}. In this notation, we may re-write the Hamiltonian as

where we have introduced the lab-fixed frame (x0,y0,z0)(x_{0},y_{0},z_{0}) for future convenience, and ∑′\sum^{\prime} indicates that we avoid the same site (n,η)=(n′,η′)(n,\eta)=(n^{\prime},\eta^{\prime}) in the summation.

It is also convenient to generalize the Fourier transform of the dipolar sum to a matrix in sublattice space:

where the summation runs over all the underlying Bravais lattice points 𝑹n{\bm{R}}_{n} except the origin if η\eta and η′\eta^{\prime} correpond to the site within the unit cell, and all points 𝑹n{\bm{R}}_{n} otherwise. As before, ση\sigma_{\eta} indicates the staggered sign, i.e., σ=1\sigma=1 for η∈A\eta\in A and σ=−1\sigma=-1 for η∈B\eta\in B. We note that ε𝒌,η​η′{\varepsilon}_{{\bm{k}},\eta\eta^{\prime}} is periodic in the Brillouin Zone (BZ) by definition, and satisfies ε𝒌,η​η′=ε−𝒌,η′​η=ε𝒌,η′​η∗{\varepsilon}_{{\bm{k}},\eta\eta^{\prime}}={\varepsilon}_{-{\bm{k}},\eta^{\prime}\eta}={\varepsilon}^{*}_{{\bm{k}},\eta^{\prime}\eta}. Next, we discuss how to compute the different hydrodynamic observables, focusing on the T=0T=0 limit for a direct comparison with iDMRG. First, to find the reduction of the ordered moment from its classical value of SS due to quantum fluctuations, we simply set h=0h=0 such that the twisted frame and the lab-fixed frame coincide, and calculate

m=ση​⟨Sn,ηx0⟩=ση​⟨Sn,ηx⟩=S−⟨an,η†​an,η⟩m=\sigma_{\eta}\langle S^{x_{0}}_{n,\eta}\rangle=\sigma_{\eta}\langle S^{x}_{n,\eta}\rangle=S-\langle a^{\dagger}_{n,\eta}a_{n,\eta}\rangle (15)

Since we only want the susceptibility as h→0h\to 0, we can evaluate ⟨am,η†​am,η⟩\langle a^{\dagger}_{m,\eta}a_{m,\eta}\rangle for h=0h=0 since the overall proportionality constant already scales as hh. =12​J​S​ε0​(S+12−14​s​N​∑𝒌∑ν=2​s+14​s[W𝒌†​W𝒌]ν,ν)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2JS{\varepsilon}_{0}}\left(S+\frac{1}{2}-\frac{1}{4sN}\sum_{{\bm{k}}}\sum_{\nu=2s+1}^{4s}[W_{\bm{k}}^{\dagger}W_{\bm{k}}]_{\nu,\nu}\right) (17)

Finally, to find the spin-wave velocity, we again set h=0h=0 and focus on the acoustic spin-wave branch μ=μ0\mu=\mu_{0} which is gapless at the Γ\Gamma-point. Generally, ω𝒌,μ=μ0≈v​|𝒌|\omega_{{\bm{k}},\mu=\mu_{0}}\approx v|{\bm{k}}| for small |𝒌||{\bm{k}}|, with vv being the corresponding spin-wave velocity which is numerically extracted by fitting the dispersion at low momenta.

To conclude this section, we note that the spin-wave dispersion obtained from LSWT (at h=0h=0) has a minimum at the Γ\Gamma-point in the BZ for the square, hexagonal, truncated square and truncated trihexagonal lattices, as expected for a Néel antiferromagnet. However, for the snub square lattice, we find that the spin-wave energy goes to zero at a finite wave-vector (see SM for a plot of the spin-wave dispersion assuming a Néel phase) and becomes imaginary near the Γ\Gamma point, indicating an instability of the Néel state [45]. To investigate this further, we carry out a Luttinger-Tisza analysis [49] of the ordering wave-vector [1]. Within this framework, the classical ground state is found by diagonalizing the Fourier transform J~​(𝒌)\tilde{J}({\bm{k}}) of the real space interaction matrix Ji​jJ_{ij} between spins: the wave-vector 𝒌LT{\bm{k}}_{\rm LT} corresponding to the minima determines the ordering pattern. We indeed find the Néel state to be the classical ground state for the four lattices where the LSWT results are meaningful.

On the other hand, as shown in Fig. 2, we find that the minimum of the Luttinger-Tisza spectrum occurs slightly displaced from the Γ\Gamma point for the snub square lattice, at some small symmetry-related incommensurate wave-vectors. This hints at the possibility that the snub square lattice can have a ground state that is different from the Néel state, which renders LSWT with the Néel state as the starting point infeasible. As for our numerical observations: at the DMRG-accessible system sizes, we always find a simple Néel-like order for the snub square ground state, but we believe it is rather plausible that the incommensuration instability only appears at larger length scales. Alternatively, it may be that strong quantum effects ultimately favor the Néel order over a classical spiral [13].

III Hydrodynamic parameters

As discussed above, the low-energy physics of the collinear U⁡(1)U(1) symmetry-breaking order phases can be described by a single-component spin wave theory. This hydrodynamic theory carries three free parameters, which, in a DMRG settting, are conveniently chosen as the magnetization, mm, spin susceptibility, χ⟂\chi_{\perp}, and spin stiffness, ρ\rho. Other characteristic quantities of this phase follow; in particular, the spin-wave velocity is given by v=ρ/χ⟂v=\sqrt{\rho/\chi_{\perp}} [27]. In this section we compute these values for the HdXYH_{\rm{dXY}} ground state on the four ordered lattices. Compared to short-range models, the 1/r31/r^{3} interactions (i) restrict the the range of system sizes which are computationally accessible, and (ii) enhance finite-size effects on the systems where we are able to reach good convergence. Consequently, the precision with which we can estimate the thermodynamic limit of these values is generally unclear. As a comparison point for the DMRG results, we will also report values analytically computed in linear spin wave theory (LSWT).

III.1 Magnetization

We first determine the bulk magnetization mm by computing the ground states of finite-size systems in the presence of a symmetry-breaking environment [73]. As depicted in Fig. 3, we take our system to be a finite-length LL central segment of a long cylinder of circumference WW. The environment (EE) spins outside this segment are fully pinned, ⟨SEx⟩=±1/2\langle S^{x}_{E}\rangle=\pm 1/2, and act as a source of a non-uniform symmetry-breaking field for the system through the dipolar XY interaction. In practice, we represent only the system spins, and use finite DMRG to find their ground state under HdXY+∑ihi​SixH_{\rm{dXY}}+\sum_{i}h_{i}S^{x}_{i}, where hi=2​∑j∈E⟨Sjx⟩/ri​j3h_{i}=2\sum_{j\in E}\langle S^{x}_{j}\rangle/r_{ij}^{3} 11 1 In this sum, we only include environment spins with ri​j<Rmaxr_{ij}<R_{\mathrm{max}}, using the same cutoff radius Rmax=W/2R_{\mathrm{max}}=W/2 as for the intrasystem spin-spin interactions.. With this setup, mm is estimated as simply the expectation value ⟨Six⟩\langle S_{i}^{x}\rangle of a central system spin away from the environment (averaged over the ring at the center of the segment). In Fig. 4, we show the DMRG spatial profile of the local magnetization as a function of the linear distance from the left edge; the magnetization at the edge is generically larger than in the bulk, simply due to the environment-generated magnetic field. In the thermodynamic limit W→∞W\to\infty (with aspect ratio L/WL/W fixed), the bulk ⟨Six⟩\langle S^{x}_{i}\rangle and other definitions of mm should converge to the same value.

The results of our calculations are summarized in Table 1, which lists the cylinder geometry, our estimate of the center-spin magnetization, mm, the largest MPS bond dimension we reach, dd, and the associated truncation error, ϵt\epsilon_{t}. For each lattice, we are able to reach good convergence on two or three cylinder sizes. For the magnetization, we compute the DMRG ground states for an increasing sequence of dd and estimate the d→∞d\to\infty limit by a linearly extrapolation of the truncation error, ϵt→0\epsilon_{t}\to 0. The linear fit error is displayed when that error is in the third significant digit; smaller errors are physically irrelevant, i.e. compared to finite-size effects. The LSWT results are within a few percent of the DMRG values.

III.2 Spin susceptibility

The second parameter we determine is the spin susceptiblity, χ⟂\chi_{\perp}. Our DMRG approach here is to compute the Anderson tower of states (TOS), that is, the lowest energy state of a finite-size system (NN total spins) in each MzM^{z} sector [71]. The zero-momentum, collective rigid rotor motion of the spins splits the energy of these states by ETOS=Mz2/2​IE_{\mathrm{TOS}}=M_{z}^{2}/2I, with an extensive moment of inertia I=χ⟂​NI=\chi_{\perp}N [52]. Thus, we return to using U⁡(1)U(1)-conserving tensors, compute ground states in the Mz=0,1,2M_{z}=0,1,2 sectors, and fit their energies to the quadratic relation E⁡(Mz)=E0+Mz2/(2​N​χ⟂).E(M_{z})=E_{0}+M_{z}^{2}/(2N\chi_{\perp}). The results are given in Table 2, with the errors representing the standard error of the fit. In this case the LSWT values are 10-30% larger (more classical) than the DMRG ones.

III.3 Spin stiffness

The final quantity we measure is the spin stiffness—the energy cost of twisted boundary conditions [51]. For this we return to iDMRG, and carry out a flux insertion experiment [32]. Explicitly, we modify couplings of the Hamiltonian according to a U⁡(1)U(1) flux θ\theta through the infinite cylinder,

HdXY[θ]=J∑i<j1ri​j3(ei​θi​jSi+Sj−+h.c.)H_{\rm{dXY}}[\theta]=J\sum_{i<j}\frac{1}{r_{ij}^{3}}\left(e^{i\theta_{ij}}S_{i}^{+}S_{j}^{-}+\mathrm{h.c.}\right) (18)

where the relative angle θi​j=(𝐫i​j⋅𝐖/W2)​θ\theta_{ij}=(\mathbf{r}_{ij}\cdot\mathbf{W}/W^{2})\theta, with 𝐖\mathbf{W} the periodic vector around the cylinder. Varying θ\theta, the energy dependence defines the spin stiffness as

ρ=W2​∂2e0∂ϕ2,\rho=W^{2}\frac{\partial^{2}e_{0}}{\partial\phi^{2}}, (19)

where e0​[θ]e_{0}[\theta] is the energy per spin of the θ\theta-dependent ground state.

We compute e0​[θ]e_{0}[\theta] for one width per each cylinder, shown in Fig. 6. The corresponding stiffness ρ\rho is listed in Table 3. In this case, the reported errors indicate the difference between calculations done at d=2048d=2048 and d=1024d=1024, which is much larger than the uncertainty in the fit to e0​[θ]e_{0}[\theta]. We also include the LSWT prediction, which is notably lower than the DMRG calculation; the largest difference is for the truncated square lattice, at about 40%.

IV Local singlet states

Local geometric frustration penalizes collinear ordering. For some lattices with complex unit cells, we find that the ground state of HdXYH_{\rm dXY} is a short-range-entangled paramagnet, where no ordering occurs at all. These are the truncated hexagonal (“Fisher”), elongated triangular (“isosnub” or “trellis”), rhombitrihexagonal (“ruby”), and snub trihexagonal (“maple leaf”) lattices. On these geometries, neighboring spins within a unit cell become strongly entangled into either two-spin or six-spin singlet states (a la benzene). These local singlets can tile across the whole plane, and the full many-body wavefunction is, to good approximation, a tensor product of them [67, 25].

Let us give three brief remarks on these local singlet states. First, this type of state is similar to a valence bond solid (VBS), but strictly speaking is not a true “solid” as no spatial symmetries are spontaneously broken. Second, this fully symmetric paramagnetic state is possible because the unit cells contain an even number of spins. Finally, we note that although our Hamiltonian is only U⁡(1)U(1) symmetric, the ground state of an antiferromagnet XY interaction between two spin-1/2 is identical to an S​U​(2)SU(2) singlet; this relation no longer holds exactly for our many-body wavefunctions, but we do find that the local correlations in this class of states are largely spin-isotropic (not shown). We comment on possible directions for further study of these paramagnets in Sec. VI.

V Triangular lattice

We now turn to the triangular lattice. Collinear order is again disfavored by geometric frustration, but on this geometry there is now no possibility of a trivial local singlet state [44, 55, 29]. One must then consider more intricate states such as non-collinear magnetic orders, valence bond solids, and quantum spin liquids. This can lead to two complications: (i) enlarged unit cells of the ordering, possibly incompatible with the numerical geometry, (ii) delicate low-energy competition between phases. Unfortunately, we find in our numerics that each rears its head here, and the second is further complicated by the long-range tail of the dipolar couplings. We thus present results showcasing the various competing phases, and leave final judgement between them as a challenge for future investigation. As a preview, in Fig. 8 we show the iDMRG spin correlations on the W=9W=9 and W=10W=10 cylinders; the first has strong symmetry-breaking correlations, while for the latter the correlations quickly decay, suggesting a possible quantum spin liquid.

V.1 Extended phase diagram

First, we locate HdXYH_{\rm{dXY}} in a broader phase diagram. Although there are no explicit free parameters in the physical Hamiltonian, numerically one can always tune the relative strengths of the various couplings. That is, we consider general XY models of the form,

HJ=∑mJm​∑i<jδ⁡(ri​j−dm)​[Si+​Sj−+Si−​Sj+]H_{J}=\sum_{m}J_{m}\sum_{i<j}\delta(r_{ij}-d_{m})\left[S_{i}^{+}S_{j}^{-}+S_{i}^{-}S_{j}^{+}\right] (20)

where dmd_{m} is the distance corresponding to mmth-nearest-neighbors on the lattice (e.g. d1=1d_{1}=1 for nearest-neighbors, d2=3d_{2}=\sqrt{3} for next-nearest-neighbors, etc.). The dipolar model HdXYH_{\rm{dXY}} obtains when these couplings decay cubically with distance, i.e. Jm=J​dm−3J_{m}=Jd_{m}^{-3}. The nearest-neighbor XY AFM is likewise J1=JJ_{1}=J, Jm>1=0J_{m>1}=0.

In Fig. 9, we show part of the HJH_{J} phase diagram close to the HdXYH_{\rm{dXY}} point, as determined by iDMRG. We fix the first three couplings to their dipolar values, (J1,J2,J3)=(1,0.192,0.125)(J_{1},J_{2},J_{3})=(1,0.192,0.125), and then tune J4,J5J_{4},J_{5} in the area surrounding the dipolar point (0.054,0.037)(0.054,0.037). The longer-range couplings are truncated, Jm>6=0J_{m>6}=0. For this parameter scan we use the infinite XC8 cylinder, which is small enough (W=4​3≈6.92W=4\sqrt{3}\approx 6.92) to get good iDMRG results without prohibitive computational cost (d=3072d=3072), while also being commensurate with the unit cells of many common orders. The half-system von Neumann entanglement entropy [Fig. 9(a)], correlation length [Fig. 9(b)], and spatial anisotropy of local correlations [Fig. 9(c)] suggest the presence of three phases all in close proximity to the rather ambiguously located HdXYH_{\rm{dXY}} point.

First, for larger J4J_{4} and smaller J5J_{5}, we find coplanar 120∘ magnetic order; the classical order parameter is revealed in a finite DMRG calculation (d=1024)(d=1024) where we add a pair of weak symmetry-breaking local fields to the edge of a cylinder [73], and observe nonzero magnetization, ⟨Six⟩\langle S_{i}^{x}\rangle and ⟨Siy⟩\langle S_{i}^{y}\rangle, throughout the bulk [Fig. 9(d,f)]. In iDMRG, we use U⁡(1)U(1)-conserving, real-coefficient MPS, for which the corresponding quantum state is a uniform superposition over all U⁡(1)U(1) symmetry breaking directions, as well as over the two possible chiralities for the ordering. This state is readily distinguished in the iDMRG phase diagram by its large correlation length, indicative of long-range off-diagonal order in S+​S−S^{+}S^{-} [Fig. 9(b)].

Second, for smaller J4J_{4} we find a state with relatively uniform short-range correlations but substantial quantum entanglement. We do not characterize this state in detail here, but we conjecture it is connected to the well-studied quantum spin liquid (QSL) phase of the triangular lattice J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} Heisenberg model [81, 36, 35, 65, 19, 37, 42].

Finally, when J4J_{4} and J5J_{5} are increased, there is a smooth crossover to a lower-entanglement state with spatially-anisotropic spin correlations, suggestive of the collinear stripe order seen in the J1J_{1}-J2J_{2} Heisenberg model. Curiously, the stripe correlations in our extended XY model are relatively short-ranged, and for the finite DMRG calculation we find that the ordering direction oscillates with a period of about ten sites [Fig 9(e,f)]. We note this stripe density wave (DW) is reminiscent of the mescoscopic ordering patterns seen in thin films with magnetic dipole-dipole interactions [18].

V.2 Luttinger-Tisza analysis

To gain some analytic insight into this phase diagram, we use the Luttinger-Tisza method to find the classical ground state of HJH_{J} [1]. Since the triangular lattice is a Bravais lattice, the interaction matrix J~​(𝒌)\tilde{J}(\bm{k}) simplifies to a single real-valued function,

J~​(𝒌,J4,J5)=∑n=15Jn​[∑icos⁡(𝒌⋅𝜹i(n))],\tilde{J}(\bm{k};J_{4},J_{5})=\sum_{n=1}^{5}J_{n}\left[\sum_{i}\cos({\bm{k}\cdot\bm{\delta}_i^{(n)}})\right], (21)

where 𝜹i(n)\bm{\delta}_{i}^{(n)} denote the vectors connecting the nthn^{\text{th}} neighbors. The ordering wavevector corresponds to the value 𝒌LT\bm{k}_{\mathrm{LT}} which minimizes J~​(𝐤)\tilde{J}(\mathbf{k}). If this momentum is shifted away from a high-symmetry point, the classical ground state takes the form of an in-plane spiral, i.e., 𝑺⁡(𝑹i)=(cos⁡((𝒌LT⋅𝑹i)),sin⁡((𝒌LT⋅𝑹i)),0)\bm{S}(\bm{R}_{i})=\left(\cos{(\bm{k}_{\mathrm{LT}}\cdot\bm{R}_i)},\sin{(\bm{k}_{\mathrm{LT}}\cdot\bm{R}_i)},0\right).

In Fig. 10, we show this classical phase diagram surrounding the dipolar point, fixing the first three couplings to their dipolar values, (J1,J2,J3)=(1,0.192,0.125)(J_{1},J_{2},J_{3})=(1,0.192,0.125), and then tuning J4,J5J_{4},J_{5} near (0.054,0.037)(0.054,0.037). We find that 𝒌LT\bm{k}_{\mathrm{LT}} lies on a line between the KK and MM points of the Brillouin zone. The KK-ordered phase in the lower-right half of the phase diagram, encompassing the dipolar point, is the familiar 120∘120^{\circ} AFM. The upper-left half of the diagram hosts an incommensurate stripe phase. We think it would be interesting for future work to clarify the relation between this classical order and the quantum state found in DMRG.

V.3 Wider cylinders

Given the murky situation suggested by the XC8 calculations, it is natural to test whether moving towards the thermodynamic limit (W→∞W\to\infty, all couplings included) affords any clarity. To this end, we calculate the iDMRG ground state on several wider cylinders [70]. In this case tuning across a phase diagram is substantially more expensive, so we restrict our focus to just the state that occurs at the dipolar point (while truncating Jm=0J_{m}=0 when dm≥W/2d_{m}\geq W/2).

Our results are summarized in Table 4, which lists the cylinder geometry, its width, WW, the number of included couplings JnJ_{n}; whether the 120∘ order is commensurate, the observed ground state order; the MPS bond dimension, dd, and truncation error, ϵt\epsilon_{t}. (For some cylinders, marked with an asterisk, we encountered better numerical stability using the single-site DMRG algorithm, which does not directly output a truncation error.) In general, we find that when the 120∘ order is commensurate, it stabilizes; when it is not, a disordered liquid results (Fig. 8). As a first glimpse towards the nature of this liquid, we compute its momentum- and spin-resolved entanglement spectrum [57, 16] on the YC10 cylinder (Fig. 11). Interestingly, we find an arc-like structure similar to that seen in the J1−J2J_{1}-J_{2} Heisenberg spin liquid [60]. This is not definitive evidence of topological character per se, but it does indicate that the local entanglement properties of the two states are similar, and suggests that they may be in the same phase. We leave a more detailed characterization to future work.

VI Outlook

In this work, we characterized the ground states of a dipolar XY Hamiltonian on nine of the eleven Archimedean lattices; the classification is completed by the square and kagome lattices in other work [11, 64, 6]. Broadly, we found that the lattices with lower geometric frustration (e.g., no frustration at the nearest neighbor level) are typically not significantly affected by the longer range of the dipolar interactions. Consequently, these lattices stabilize the conventional bipartite Néel antiferromagnet as the ground state. Furthermore, linear spin-wave theory is able for these to provide a good match to the numerics. Looking forward, we note that for these ordered phases one can go beyond mean-field linear spin-wave theory and, for example, analytically extract the spin-wave decay-rates [80, 79, 40]. This would potentially be directly relevant for experiments, which can locally probe the real-time dynamics of spin-waves, e.g. following a quantum quench [12].

There are also three lattice geometries that we believe are deserving of further study; all three are frustrated at the nearest-neighbor level. First, the snub square lattice, which we found to be a Néel state in DMRG, but possibly an ultimately unstable one as indicated by our analytic calculations. Second, the snub trihexagonal (maple leaf) lattice, which in our computation seems to have a trivial paramagnet ground state, but in other works (with different Hamiltonians), is considered to be a likely host for quantum spin liquids [66, 20]. Finally, the ordinary triangular lattice: on this geometry, the dipolar Hamiltonian lies in a region of tight competition between three complex phases. For each of these geometries, we think it would be interesting to apply different numerical methods, and develop more sophisticated analytic theories.

To conclude, we note from the experimental side there are various accessible perturbations that could induce novel physics on any of the eleven Archimedean lattices. One pragmatic direction is to investigate whether new phases appear in the presence of a uniform magnetic field [39]. A more distinctive possibility of ultracold atom and molecule experiments, compared to the solid state, is the ability to strongly drive the system with time-varying and site-specific fields [10, 24, 7, 72, 48]. Could one use this to stabilize non-equilibrium steady states with novel emergent properties [61], even when the equilibrium ground states is a conventional antiferromagnet or a featureless paramagnet? Last but not least, because the lattice geometry itself is highly tunable in these experiments, it seems quite natural to study the effects of controlled geometric deformations on the ground state of the unadorned dipolar XY Hamiltonian [68, 54, 78].

Appendix A Details on linear spin-wave theory

In this section, we provide the derivation of the spin-wave Hamiltonian in the canted reference frame when an out-of-plane magnetic field hh is present. To this end, we first re-write the Hamiltonian H=HdXY−h​∑iSiz0H=H_{\rm dXY}-h\sum_{i}S_{i}^{z_{0}}, given in the lab-fixed frame (x0,y0,z0)(x_{0},y_{0},z_{0}), in the twisted reference frame which is rotated by an angle θη=ση​θ\theta_{\eta}=\sigma_{\eta}\theta about the y0y_{0}-axis (ση=1\sigma_{\eta}=1 for type A, and ση=−1\sigma_{\eta}=-1 for type B sublattice points.) We fix the angle θ\theta by demanding that the effective field along the (rotated) zz direction vanishes in the Hamiltonian re-written in the twisted reference frame:

H=\displaystyle H= J​∑(n,η),(n′,η′)′Sn,ηx​Sn′,η′x​cos​θη​cos​θη′+Sn,ηz​Sn′,η′z​sin​θη​sin​θη′+Sn,ηy​Sn′,η′y−2​Sn,ηz​Sn′,η′x​sin​θη​cos​θη′|𝑹n+𝒖η−𝑹n′−𝒖η′|3\displaystyle J\sum^{\prime}_{(n,\eta),(n^{\prime},\eta^{\prime})}\frac{S^{x}_{n,\eta}S^{x}_{n^{\prime},\eta^{\prime}}\cos\theta_{\eta}\cos\theta_{\eta^{\prime}}+S^{z}_{n,\eta}S^{z}_{n^{\prime},\eta^{\prime}}\sin\theta_{\eta}\sin\theta_{\eta^{\prime}}+S^{y}_{n,\eta}S^{y}_{n^{\prime},\eta^{\prime}}-2S^{z}_{n,\eta}S^{x}_{n^{\prime},\eta^{\prime}}\sin\theta_{\eta}\cos\theta_{\eta^{\prime}}}{|{\bm{R}}_{n}+{\bm{u}}_{\eta}-{\bm{R}}_{n^{\prime}}-{\bm{u}}_{\eta^{\prime}}|^{3}}
−h∑(n,η)(Sn,ηzcosθη+Sn,ηxsinθη)\displaystyle~~~-h\sum_{(n,\eta)}(S^{z}_{n,\eta}\cos\theta_{\eta}+S^{x}_{n,\eta}\sin\theta_{\eta}) (22)

Collecting the terms proportional to Sn,ηzS^{z}_{n,\eta} and taking the classical expectation value of the remaining operators involved (i.e., Sn,η′x→⟨Sn,η′x⟩=ση′​SS^{x}_{n,\eta^{\prime}}\to\langle S^{x}_{n,\eta^{\prime}}\rangle=\sigma_{\eta^{\prime}}S and Sn,η′z→⟨Sn,η′z⟩=0S^{z}_{n,\eta^{\prime}}\to\langle S^{z}_{n,\eta^{\prime}}\rangle=0), we can find the effective field along the zz direction in the twisted reference frame.

H⊃∑n,ηhn,ηeffSn,ηz, where hn,ηeff=−2J∑n′,η′′⟨Sn′,η′x⟩​sin⁡θη​cos​θη′|𝑹n+𝒖η−𝑹n′−𝒖η′|3−hcosθη=(2JSε0−h)cosθ\displaystyle H\supset\sum_{n,\eta}h^{\rm eff}_{n,\eta}S^{z}_{n,\eta},\text{ where }h^{\rm eff}_{n,\eta}=-2J\sum^{\prime}_{n^{\prime},\eta^{\prime}}\frac{\langle S^{x}_{n^{\prime},\eta^{\prime}}\rangle\sin\theta_{\eta}\cos\theta_{\eta^{\prime}}}{|{\bm{R}}_{n}+{\bm{u}}_{\eta}-{\bm{R}}_{n^{\prime}}-{\bm{u}}_{\eta^{\prime}}|^{3}}-h\cos\theta_{\eta}=\left(2JS{\varepsilon}_{0}-h\right)\cos\theta (23)

where we have used that ⟨Sn′,η′x⟩=ση′​S\langle S^{x}_{n^{\prime},\eta^{\prime}}\rangle=\sigma_{\eta^{\prime}}S, cos⁡(θη)=cos⁡(θ)\cos(\theta_\eta)=\cos(\theta) and sin⁡(θη)=sin⁡(ση​θ)=ση​sin⁡(θ)\sin(\theta_{\eta})=\sin(\sigma_\eta\theta)=\sigma_{\eta}\sin(\theta), and also used the definition of the dipolar sum ε0{\varepsilon}_{0} from the main text. This gives us the expression for the canting angle θ\theta via setting hn,ηeff=0h^{\rm eff}_{n,\eta}=0, yielding

sin⁡θ=h2​J​S​ε0,\sin\theta=\frac{h}{2JS{\varepsilon}_{0}}, (24)

which is Eq. (6) in the main text. On choosing the canting angle θ\theta as above, the Hamiltonian in the twisted reference frame takes the following form

H=J​∑(n,η),(n′,η′)′Sn,ηx​Sn′,η′x​cos​θη​cos​θη′+Sn,ηz​Sn′,η′z​sin​θη​sin​θη′+Sn,ηy​Sn′,η′y|𝑹n+𝒖η−𝑹n′−𝒖η′|3−h​∑(n,η)Sn,ηx​sin⁡θηH=J\sum^{\prime}_{(n,\eta),(n^{\prime},\eta^{\prime})}\frac{S^{x}_{n,\eta}S^{x}_{n^{\prime},\eta^{\prime}}\cos\theta_{\eta}\cos\theta_{\eta^{\prime}}+S^{z}_{n,\eta}S^{z}_{n^{\prime},\eta^{\prime}}\sin\theta_{\eta}\sin\theta_{\eta^{\prime}}+S^{y}_{n,\eta}S^{y}_{n^{\prime},\eta^{\prime}}}{|{\bm{R}}_{n}+{\bm{u}}_{\eta}-{\bm{R}}_{n^{\prime}}-{\bm{u}}_{\eta^{\prime}}|^{3}}-h\sum_{(n,\eta)}S^{x}_{n,\eta}\sin\theta_{\eta} (25)

Now, we express the Hamiltonian in Eq. (25) in terms of linearized Holstein-Primakoff bosons defined as follows:

Sn,ηx=ση​(S−an,η†​an,η),Sn,ηy=2​S2​i​(an,η†−an,η)​ση,Sn,ηz=2​S2​(an,η†+an,η)S^{x}_{n,\eta}=\sigma_{\eta}(S-a^{\dagger}_{n,\eta}a_{n,\eta}),~S^{y}_{n,\eta}=\frac{\sqrt{2S}}{2i}(a^{\dagger}_{n,\eta}-a_{n,\eta})\sigma_{\eta},~S^{z}_{n,\eta}=\frac{\sqrt{2S}}{2}(a^{\dagger}_{n,\eta}+a_{n,\eta}) (26)

Plugging Eq. (26) into Eq. (25) and neglecting all cubic and higher order terms, we have

H=\displaystyle H= J​S2​cos2⁡θ⁡(∑(n,η),(n′,η′)′ση​ση′|𝑹n−𝑹n′+𝒖η−𝒖η′|3)−J​S​cos2⁡θ⁡(∑(n,η),(n′,η′)′ση​ση′​(an,η†​an,η+an′,η′†​an′,η′)|𝑹n−𝑹n′+𝒖η−𝒖η′|3)\displaystyle\,JS^{2}\cos^{2}\theta\left(\sum^{\prime}_{(n,\eta),(n^{\prime},\eta^{\prime})}\frac{\sigma_{\eta}\sigma_{\eta^{\prime}}}{|{\bm{R}}_{n}-{\bm{R}}_{n^{\prime}}+{\bm{u}}_{\eta}-{\bm{u}}_{\eta^{\prime}}|^{3}}\right)-JS\cos^{2}\theta\left(\sum^{\prime}_{(n,\eta),(n^{\prime},\eta^{\prime})}\frac{\sigma_{\eta}\sigma_{\eta^{\prime}}(a^{\dagger}_{n,\eta}a_{n,\eta}+a^{\dagger}_{n^{\prime},\eta^{\prime}}a_{n^{\prime},\eta^{\prime}})}{|{\bm{R}}_{n}-{\bm{R}}_{n^{\prime}}+{\bm{u}}_{\eta}-{\bm{u}}_{\eta^{\prime}}|^{3}}\right)
−J​S​cos2⁡θ2​(∑(n,η),(n′,η′)′ση​ση′​(an,η†​an′,η′†+an,η​an′,η′)|𝑹n−𝑹n′+𝒖η−𝒖η′|3)+J​S​(1+sin2​θ)2​(∑(n,η),(n′,η′)′ση​ση′​(an,η​an′,η′†+an,η†​an′,η′)|𝑹n−𝑹n′+𝒖η−𝒖η′|3)\displaystyle-\frac{JS\cos^{2}\theta}{2}\left(\sum^{\prime}_{(n,\eta),(n^{\prime},\eta^{\prime})}\frac{\sigma_{\eta}\sigma_{\eta^{\prime}}(a^{\dagger}_{n,\eta}a^{\dagger}_{n^{\prime},\eta^{\prime}}+a_{n,\eta}a_{n^{\prime},\eta^{\prime}})}{|{\bm{R}}_{n}-{\bm{R}}_{n^{\prime}}+{\bm{u}}_{\eta}-{\bm{u}}_{\eta^{\prime}}|^{3}}\right)+\frac{JS(1+\sin^{2}\theta)}{2}\left(\sum^{\prime}_{(n,\eta),(n^{\prime},\eta^{\prime})}\frac{\sigma_{\eta}\sigma_{\eta^{\prime}}(a_{n,\eta}a^{\dagger}_{n^{\prime},\eta^{\prime}}+a^{\dagger}_{n,\eta}a_{n^{\prime},\eta^{\prime}})}{|{\bm{R}}_{n}-{\bm{R}}_{n^{\prime}}+{\bm{u}}_{\eta}-{\bm{u}}_{\eta^{\prime}}|^{3}}\right)
−h​sin⁡θ⁡(∑n,η(S−an,η†​an,η))\displaystyle-h\sin\theta\left(\sum_{n,\eta}(S-a^{\dagger}_{n,\eta}a_{n,\eta})\right) (27)

Note that we do not have any linear term in the HP bosons in the Hamiltonian in Eq. (27), the condition that the effective field on any spin vanishes is essentially an energy minimization condition which gets rid of these linear terms.

Finally, we write the Hamiltonian in Eq. (27) in terms of the Fourier transformed HP bosons, leading to

H\displaystyle H =HcAFM(0)+H(2), where\displaystyle=H^{(0)}_{\rm cAFM}+H^{(2)},\text{ where}
HcAFM(0)\displaystyle H^{(0)}_{\rm cAFM} =−2​s​N​[J​S​(S+1)​ε0​cos2​θ+h⁡(S+12)​sin⁡θ]=−2​s​N​[J​S​(S+1)​ε0+h24​J​ε0]\displaystyle=-2sN\left[JS(S+1){\varepsilon}_{0}\cos^{2}\theta+h\left(S+\frac{1}{2}\right)\sin\theta\right]=-2sN\left[JS(S+1){\varepsilon}_{0}+\frac{h^{2}}{4J{\varepsilon}_{0}}\right]
H(2)\displaystyle H^{(2)} =J​S2​∑𝒌,η,η′[2​ε0​δη​η′−(1+sin2​θ)​ε𝒌,η,η′]​(a𝒌,η†​a𝒌,η′+a−𝒌,η​a−𝒌,η′†)+cos2​θ​ε𝒌,η​η′​(a−𝒌,η​a𝒌,η′+a𝒌,η†​a−𝒌,η′†),\displaystyle=\frac{JS}{2}\sum_{{\bm{k}},\eta,\eta^{\prime}}\left[2{\varepsilon}_{0}\,\delta_{\eta\eta^{\prime}}-(1+\sin^{2}\theta){\varepsilon}_{{\bm{k}},\eta,\eta^{\prime}}\right]\left(a^{\dagger}_{{\bm{k}},\eta}a_{{\bm{k}},\eta^{\prime}}+a_{-{\bm{k}},\eta}a^{\dagger}_{-{\bm{k}},\eta^{\prime}}\right)+\cos^{2}\theta\,{\varepsilon}_{{\bm{k}},\eta\eta^{\prime}}\left(a_{-{\bm{k}},\eta}a_{{\bm{k}},\eta^{\prime}}+a^{\dagger}_{{\bm{k}},\eta}a^{\dagger}_{-{\bm{k}},\eta^{\prime}}\right), (28)

which is Eq. (9) in the main text.

Finally, we present the spin-wave spectra ω𝒌,μ\omega_{{\bm{k}},\mu} for the 2​s2s spin-wave branches in Fig. 12, obtained by diagonalizing H(2)H^{(2)} via a paraunitary matrix W𝒌W_{\bm{k}} as detailed in the main text. Evidently, the hexagonal, truncated trihexagonal and truncated square lattices all show an acoustic mode μ0\mu_{0} that disperses linearly at low-energy, i.e., ω𝒌,μ0≈vμ0​|𝒌|\omega_{{\bm{k}},\mu_{0}}\approx v_{\mu_{0}}|{\bm{k}}| near the Γ\Gamma-point. However, the snub square lattice shows that the spin-wave energy becomes imaginary near the Γ\Gamma-point, indicative of an instability of the Néel state as discussed in the main text.

Appendix B Out-of-plane susceptibility χ⟂\chi_{\perp} in linear spin-wave theory

Here, we derive the equation for susceptibility of the ordered antiferromagnetic Néel phases to an out-of-plane magnetic field hh. We note from the main text that the total magnetization Mz0M_{z_{0}} in the z0z_{0}-direction is given by

Mz0=∑(n,η)⟨Sn,ηz0⟩=∑(n,η)(⟨Sn,ηz⟩​cos⁡θη+⟨Sn,ηx⟩​sin⁡θη)=sin⁡θ​∑(n,η)(S−⟨an,η†​an,η⟩)=h2​J​S​ε0​∑(n,η)(S−⟨an,η†​an,η⟩)M_{z_{0}}=\sum_{(n,\eta)}\langle S^{z_{0}}_{n,\eta}\rangle=\sum_{(n,\eta)}\left(\langle S^{z}_{n,\eta}\rangle\cos\theta_{\eta}+\langle S^{x}_{n,\eta}\rangle\sin\theta_{\eta}\right)=\sin\theta\sum_{(n,\eta)}(S-\langle a^{\dagger}_{n,\eta}a_{n,\eta}\rangle)=\frac{h}{2JS{\varepsilon}_{0}}\sum_{(n,\eta)}(S-\langle a^{\dagger}_{n,\eta}a_{n,\eta}\rangle) (29)

where we have used that ⟨Sn,ηz⟩=0\langle S^{z}_{n,\eta}\rangle=0 within linear-spin wave theory as it is made of operators that are linear in aa-bosons. The first term in Eq. (29) is just the classical value, and the second term represents the reduction due to quantum fluctuations. Since we want the differential susceptibility as h→0h\to 0, i.e., χ⟂∝∂hMz0|h→0\chi_{\perp}\propto\partial_{h}M_{z_{0}}|_{h\to 0}, we may evaluate the average HP boson occupancy ⟨an,η†​an,η⟩\langle a^{\dagger}_{n,\eta}a_{n,\eta}\rangle for h=0h=0 since the overall proportionality constant already scales as hh.

To derive a compact expression for the boson occupancy, it is convenient to move to Fourier space. Using the transformation W𝒌W_{\bm{k}} used to diagonalize H(2)H^{(2)}, we may write a𝒌,ηa_{{\bm{k}},\eta} in terms of γ𝒌,μ\gamma_{{\bm{k}},\mu} and calculate the susceptibility as h(2)h^{(2)} is diagonal in the number operator for γ𝒌,μ\gamma_{{\bm{k}},\mu} bosons, as follows:

∑m,η⟨am,η†​am,η⟩\displaystyle\sum_{m,\eta}\langle a^{\dagger}_{m,\eta}a_{m,\eta}\rangle =∑𝒌,η⟨a𝒌,η†​a𝒌,η⟩=12​∑𝒌,η(⟨a𝒌,η†​a𝒌,η⟩+⟨a−𝒌,η†​a−𝒌,η⟩)\displaystyle=\sum_{{\bm{k}},\eta}\langle a^{\dagger}_{{\bm{k}},\eta}a_{{\bm{k}},\eta}\rangle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{{\bm{k}},\eta}(\langle a^{\dagger}_{{\bm{k}},\eta}a_{{\bm{k}},\eta}\rangle+\langle a^{\dagger}_{-{\bm{k}},\eta}a_{-{\bm{k}},\eta}\rangle)

=(12​∑𝒌⟨Ψ𝒌†​Ψ𝒌⟩)−2​N​s2\displaystyle=\left(\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\bm{k}}\langle\Psi^{\dagger}_{\bm{k}}\Psi_{\bm{k}}\rangle\right)-\frac{2Ns}{2}
=(12​∑𝒌⟨Γ𝒌†​W𝒌†​W𝒌​Γ𝒌⟩)−N​s\displaystyle=\left(\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\bm{k}}\langle\Gamma^{\dagger}_{\bm{k}}W_{\bm{k}}^{\dagger}W_{\bm{k}}\Gamma_{\bm{k}}\rangle\right)-Ns
=12​∑𝒌[∑ν=12​s[W𝒌†​W𝒌]ν,ν​nB​(ω𝒌,ν)+∑ν=2​s+14​s[W𝒌†​W𝒌]ν,ν​(1+nB​(ω𝒌,ν))]−N​s\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{{\bm{k}}}\left[\sum_{\nu=1}^{2s}[W_{\bm{k}}^{\dagger}W_{\bm{k}}]_{\nu,\nu}~n_{B}(\omega_{{\bm{k}},\nu})+\sum_{\nu=2s+1}^{4s}[W_{\bm{k}}^{\dagger}W_{\bm{k}}]_{\nu,\nu}\left(1+n_{B}(\omega_{{\bm{k}},\nu})\right)\right]-Ns (30)

Appendix C Luttinger-Tisza analysis

In this section, we provide a brief overview of the Luttinger-Tizsa analysis [49] that is used in the main text. We begin by representing the quantum XY-model spins as classical two-dimensional vectors with unit length, with the Hamiltoninan taking the general form,

H=12​∑n,n′∑η,η′Jn​n′η,η′​𝑺n,η⋅𝑺n′,η′,H=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{n,n^{\prime}}\sum_{\eta,\eta^{\prime}}J_{nn^{\prime}}^{\eta,\eta^{\prime}}\bm{S}_{n,\eta}\cdot\bm{S}_{n^{\prime},\eta^{\prime}}, (32)

where n,n′n,n^{\prime} denote the Bravias lattice positions and η,η′\eta,\eta^{\prime} denote the sublattice labels. The method proceeds by writing the Hamiltonian in momentum space by defining

𝑺n,η=1N​∑𝒌𝑺~𝒌η​ei​𝒌⋅𝑹n\bm{S}_{n,\eta}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_{\bm{k}}\tilde{\bm{S}}_{\bm{k}}^{\eta}e^{i\bm{k}\cdot\bm{R}_{n}} (33)

The Hamiltonian can thus be written as

H=∑𝒌∑η,η′J~η​η′​(𝒌)​𝑺~−𝒌η​𝑺~𝒌η′, where ​J~η​η′​(𝒌)=12​∑𝑹nJη​η′​(𝑹n)​ei​𝒌⋅𝑹nH=\sum_{\bm{k}}\sum_{\eta,\eta^{\prime}}\tilde{J}^{\eta\eta^{\prime}}(\bm{k})\tilde{\bm{S}}_{-\bm{k}}^{\eta}\tilde{\bm{S}}_{\bm{k}}^{\eta^{\prime}},\text{ where }\tilde{J}^{\eta\eta^{\prime}}(\bm{k})=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\bm{R}_{n}}J^{\eta\eta^{\prime}}(\bm{R}_{n})\,e^{i\bm{k}\cdot\bm{R}_{n}} (34)

is the Fourier-transformed interaction matrix in the sublattice space. This becomes a quadratic form for which one needs to find the spin configuration that minimizes the energy, subject to the unit length constraint on each spin (strong constraint) that makes the problem analytically intractable on most lattices. The Luttinger-Tisza insight is to relax this constraint to the weak constraint as a necessary (but not sufficient) condition that the strong constraint is followed,

∑n,η|𝑺n​η|2=N​Ns,\sum_{n,\eta}|\bm{S}_{n\eta}|^{2}=NN_{s}, (35)

or, equivalently in momentum space:

∑𝒌∑η|𝑺𝒌η|2=N​Ns,\sum_{\bm{k}}\sum_{\eta}|\bm{S}^{\eta}_{\bm{k}}|^{2}=NN_{s}, (36)

where NN is the number of unit cells and NsN_{s} is the number of sublattices in each unit cell. The problem of minimization simplifies into an eigenvalue problem, and then one needs to check if the strong constraint is satisfied to declare a solution is found. Writing Eq. (34) in matrix notation, we have,

H=∑𝒌S~𝒌†​J~​(𝒌)​S~𝒌=∑𝒌∑ν=1Nsλν​(𝒌)​|𝜻ν​𝒌|2H=\sum_{\bm{k}}\tilde{S}_{\bm{k}}^{\dagger}\tilde{J}({\bm{k}})\tilde{S}_{\bm{k}}=\sum_{\bm{k}}\sum_{\nu=1}^{N_{s}}\lambda_{\nu}(\bm{k})|\bm{\zeta}_{\nu\bm{k}}|^{2} (37)

The energy is minimized while simultaneously satisfying the weak constraint only if the mode with the minimum eigenvalue λmin​(𝒌L​T)\lambda_{\mathrm{min}}(\bm{k}_{LT}) is allowed.

We checked numerically that this method gives the Néel states as the classical ground states (i.e. the strong constraint is also satisfied) for the the three lattices where LSWT works. On the other hand, the sunb square lattice has 𝒌L​T\bm{k}_{LT} which deviates from the Gamma point and lies at an incommensurate point along the Γ−M\Gamma-M line (and the other momenta related by the C4C_{4} symmetry). The minimum wave-vector moving away from the Γ\Gamma point hints at a different classical ground state on the snub square lattice. These results are presented in Fig. 2 in the main text.
